headline: The False Comfort of Online Shopping

paragraphs.text: This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight. Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning.

Between Black Friday deals, holiday gift guides, and the endless stream of targeted ads, it’s hard to avoid the temptation to buy something right now. And with just a few taps on our phones, we can purchase almost anything without having to leave the couch. Shopping has never been easier—or more solitary.

In a new essay, Lily Meyer revisits Sophie Kinsella’s Confessions of a Shopaholic, 25 years after its publication in the United States, to explore how shopping has become an ever more isolating activity. The novel’s protagonist spends much of her time wandering through stores, accumulating debt. But at least her shopping takes place in the company of other people. Today, much of that experience has moved online, where influencers recommend products with the familiar tone of a friend, even as their relationships with followers remain fundamentally commercial. Meyer argues that modern shopping doesn't just isolate us from others; it can also create the illusion of companionship, blurring the line between genuine connection and consumption. Her essay offers a reminder that shopping can’t substitute for human connection.
The Loneliness of Buying Too Many Things
Confessions of a Shopaholic, 25 years later, suggests that the way we buy things has gotten too isolated.
It’s never been more exhausting to buy stuff.
It’s Too Easy to Buy Stuff You Don’t Want
Online shopping is too fast for good decisions. (From 2023)
